attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: The sentence says only that paying demand is 'unclear'. It voices uncertainty, not a testable fact about customers. The hypothetical installation clause is kept. It is better treated as rhetoric than as a scorable observation.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to turn hedged uncertainty into a binary claim. Scoring it would mean picking an analyst forecast, a capacity universe and a period, none of which the speaker gave.

reviews.rationale: 'It's unclear who would pay' is a hedged statement of uncertainty. It names no forecast, quantity or period. No fair support or contradiction test exists, and the packet has no outcome evidence. The claim is not adjudicable.

attribution.note: Zitron restates his own earlier estimate in first person ('I estimate').

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the $374B construction-in-progress total and the $200B-or-more GPU estimate. It drops 'primarily from NVIDIA', a minor omission. 'I estimate' is a firm estimate, not a probabilistic hedge.

contract.note: Using each company's latest disclosed balance and the population from his earlier piece is a fair reading. The contract also requires a GPU-only breakdown, which is fair.

evidence.note: Alphabet Q2 2026 10-Q defines assets not yet in service. It gives no GPU breakdown and covers one company, so it cannot settle the aggregate.
Its five-company total is $250.2B, and Microsoft does not disclose the line. The sample is smaller than Zitron's population, so it does not contradict the claim. It gives no GPU split.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no complete aggregation for Zitron's population of companies and no GPU-only breakdown. Zeever's smaller sample ($250.2B, five firms) neither confirms nor refutes a total above $374B. Neither the total nor the $200B GPU share can be verified, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the core causal claim: soaring borrowing costs worsen data-center economics. It omits the Treasury-above-5% element, but the contract restores it. 'Nobody can measure' is rhetorical.

contract.note: Reading 'skyrocketing' as a sharp increase in marginal financing costs across several borrowers is an ordinary reading. So is the Oct 13–20 window. Treating the measurement line as rhetoric is fair.

evidence.note: Spreads widened for all eight AI borrowers between Oct 8 and Oct 15. The median rose about 79bp, while the high-yield benchmark moved 1bp, and CoreWeave rose 191bp by Oct 16. This shows a sharp, sector-specific repricing of new borrowing costs.
The 10-year Treasury was at 5.09% on Oct 16 and 5.15% on Oct 19, both above 5% within the window.

Links credit stress to execution delays, uncertain returns and rising financing costs for new projects. It also notes that built, operating assets are holding up relatively well, which limits a universal reading.

reviews.rationale: Within the window, spreads widened sharply for every sampled AI borrower against a flat high-yield benchmark, and the 10-year yield stayed above 5%. Reporting ties the repricing to project and return risk and to costlier new financing. That meets the contract. Limits: the sample is high-yield borrowers, completed assets diverge, and no change in realized profitability was measured.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence and calculation framing.

semantics.note: 'Seems unlikely' qualifies whether the drop happens; the drafter wrongly lists it as an antecedent. The claim is index arithmetic on current weights, not a forecast. Replacing the named nine-stock basket with 'major AI-trade stocks' loses the scope, which matters given the Microsoft discrepancy.

contract.note: Treating it as a publication-date weight calculation against April 14, 2000 is an ordinary reading of 'same effect'. The contract tests both Microsoft baskets and both indexes, which is fair. The mechanical-only reading excludes contagion, which the speaker never specified.

evidence.note: SPY weights from Oct 13 and Oct 21, not Oct 20. The basket differs (it adds Microsoft and Palantir), and it covers neither Oracle's weight nor the Nasdaq Composite. It cannot decide the calculation.

reviews.rationale: Testing the claim needs verified Oct 20 constituent weights for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, plus an independent record of the April 14, 2000 losses. The packet has neither. Its only weights source is for other dates, a different basket and one index, so the outcome is unresolved.
